questions.q: Benzoic acid is treated in sequence with (i) SOCl₂, (ii) excess CH₂N₂, (iii) Ag₂O, H₂O, heat. The final product is:
questions.explain: Arndt–Eistert synthesis adds one CH₂ between the R group and COOH, so C₆H₅COOH becomes C₆H₅CH₂COOH. Only one carbon is added, so 3-phenylpropanoic acid is wrong.

questions.q: Why is an excess of diazomethane used in the Arndt–Eistert synthesis?
options: To remove the HCl formed, which would otherwise convert the diazoketone into R–CO–CH₂Cl
To methylate the carboxylic acid before it reacts with SOCl₂
To act as the catalyst for the Wolff rearrangement
To reduce the ketene to an aldehyde
questions.explain: The second equivalent of CH₂N₂ destroys HCl as CH₃Cl + N₂; with too little diazomethane the HCl gives the unwanted chloromethyl ketone. Ag(I), heat or light, not CH₂N₂, drives the Wolff step.

questions.q: The Wolff rearrangement of an α-diazoketone R–CO–CHN₂ with Ag₂O gives which intermediate?
questions.explain: N₂ is lost and R shifts from the carbonyl carbon to the neighbouring carbon, giving the ketene R–CH=C=O, which water converts into RCH₂COOH. An isocyanate is the product of the Curtius rearrangement, where the shift is to nitrogen.

questions.q: Which statement about the Arndt–Eistert synthesis is NOT correct?
options: A chiral migrating group keeps its configuration
Acetic acid can equally be stepped up to propanoic acid by making BrCH₂COOH and treating it with CH₃MgBr
Trapping the ketene with ethanol gives the homologous ethyl ester
The Wolff step can be induced by Ag(I), heat or UV light
questions.explain: CH₃MgBr reacts first with the acidic COOH proton, giving methane, so no C–C bond forms; that route fails. The other three statements are true features of the Arndt–Eistert sequence.
